newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Ruehe says has Waigel pledge on Eurofighter.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Ruehe says has Waigel pledge on Eurofighter.

text.p: German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said he had gained assurances on Wednesday from Finance Minister Theo Waigel that funds for German participation in the four-nation Eurofighter project would be approved next month.

Speaking to reporters after meeting British Defence Minister George Robertson, Ruehe said he expected a decision on July 11, when the cabinet is due to consider next year's budget, and maintained his position that the project would go ahead.

Ruehe dismissed suggestions that Bonn, facing budgetary pressure, would be forced to drop out and cancel plans to buy 180 of the high-tech fighter jets, which he said were desperately needed to modernise the German air force.

"I talked to the German finance minister and he assured me there would be no problems with regards to a decision (on Eurofighter)," Ruehe said after the meeting in the military section of Cologne-Bonn airport.
"We are working on this issue and we are sure we will come to a successful solution.
"Politically, technically and internationally this is the right time for the project. But is a 20-year project and it must have a solid financial basis," Ruehe said.
Robertson told reporters he felt reassured that Bonn would honour its pledge to buy the jets and provide cash needed to start serial production, which has been delayed by political wrangling in Bonn.

"We want to move forward as quickly as possible. Ruehe says the German government wants this as well. The important thing is that the project works," said Robertson, on his first visit to Germany since taking office last month.
Britain hopes that Germany can overcome problems which have hampered development of the four-nation project, which holds the key to thousands of British jobs.

After months of delay as Germany struggles to tighten its finances to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999, Ruehe's remarks were the latest sign that Bonn might find the cash.
The jet is being jointly developed by Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (Dasa), British Aerospace, Spain's CASA and Italy's Alenia.

The head of the Eurofighter consortium in Germany, Aloysius Rauen, warned Bonn that if its decision on funding stretched beyond July it would pull out of the project -- a move that would hit workers at all Dasa production plants concerned.
"If the political decision on Eurofighter is further delayed, the industry must start phasing out production," Rauen told a news conference earlier.
Eberhard Birke, business manager of Germany's BDLI Federal Aerospace Industry Association, said the other German firms involved in the project had lost patience.

"The industry is definitely no longer in a position to continue investing in a multi-million mark project using its own resources without the slightest assurance the programme will actually take place," Birke said.

Ruehe has already offered to provide a billion marks from his own budget, which was severely scaled back last year, if Waigel comes up with another billion needed to assure that production of the jet can start.
The project will cost Germany a total 23 billion marks ($13.3 billion).
Waigel said he could find the cash by redirecting state aid set aside for the Airbus passenger jet consortium and paying it back later.
Rauen said Dasa was prepared to accept the plan but wanted to be sure Bonn was going ahead with it.
